oneSentence: Summarisation produces a shorter version of text or speech that keeps the main points and drops less important detail.
plainExplanation:
Summarisation takes a long piece of content as input and returns a shorter version. The input might be an article, meeting notes, a report, a speech transcript, or several documents on the same topic. The output is not the whole original. It is a compressed version that tries to keep the main ideas.

A system does this by finding what seems most important. In simple systems, that may mean selecting key sentences from the original text. In more advanced systems, it may mean generating new sentences that restate the main points. A transcript is a written record of spoken words. A model is a statistical system trained to detect patterns in data.

This is different from translation, which changes language, and different from text generation in general, which can create new text with no source document. Summarisation starts from source material and aims to stay close to it. It is also different from topic modelling, which groups themes rather than producing a readable short version.

The main risk is loss or distortion. Important detail can be left out. A summary can overstate one point, miss uncertainty, or add wording that was not supported by the source. So a summary is useful for triage and first reading, but not a substitute for checking the original when accuracy matters.

everydayAnalogy.title: A colleague briefs you before a meeting
everydayAnalogy.story: A team in Nairobi, Bangkok and Bogotá shares ten pages of background notes before a call. One colleague reads them and says, "Here are the three points you need before we start: the budget changed, the deadline moved, and one partner has not replied yet." That briefing saves time because nobody has to hear every paragraph first. But if someone needs the exact wording of an agreement, they still have to open the full notes.

mapping.aiElement: the original long text or transcript

mapping.analogyElement: choosing only the most important updates
checking the full notes for exact wording
mapping.aiElement: verifying the source when precision matters

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A human colleague may use wider context, shared history and judgement about what each listener needs. A summarisation system usually relies mainly on patterns in the source text and training data. It may miss nuance, uncertainty or implied meaning, and some systems copy sentences while others rewrite them, so the process is less flexible than the analogy suggests.

visual.title: From long document to short summary
visual.learningObjective: Show how summarisation turns a long source into a shorter text by selecting and compressing the most important information.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram with four boxes: source text, split into units, rank important content, produce summary. Read from left to right to see what goes in, what the system does, and what comes out. Small callouts show that some systems copy key sentences while others rewrite them.

steps.label: 1. Source text enters
steps.explanation: The input may be a report, article, transcript or several related documents.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a tall document icon on the left with many horizontal lines. Add small tags such as report, article and transcript.

steps.label: 2. Break into pieces
steps.explanation: The system analyses sentences or sections so it can compare them.
steps.visualInstruction: Show the tall document splitting into stacked cards labelled sentence 1, sentence 2, sentence 3 and section notes.

steps.label: 3. Find what matters most
steps.explanation: The system scores which parts seem central, repeated or informative.
steps.visualInstruction: Place a ranking panel in the centre with bars of different lengths beside the cards. Highlight the top items in a darker colour.

steps.label: 4. Produce a shorter version
steps.explanation: The output may copy the best sentences or rewrite them into a compact summary.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw two small paths merging into one summary card on the right: one path labelled select sentences, one labelled rewrite. The final card has three short lines.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each stage to reveal a plain-language note and an example of what is kept or dropped.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram explains summarisation as a four-step flow. First, a long source text enters, such as a report, article or transcript. Second, the text is broken into smaller pieces like sentences or sections. Third, the system ranks those pieces to estimate which ones carry the main information. Fourth, it produces a shorter output. Some systems do this by selecting sentences from the original text. Others rewrite the content into new sentences. The key idea is that the summary starts from a source and tries to preserve its main points in less space.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static left-to-right diagram shows four labelled boxes connected by arrows: source text, break into pieces, rank importance, produce summary. A note under the final box says the output may be extracted from the source or rewritten.

workedExample.scenario: Summarising a short internal news brief for busy readers
workedExample.input: Original text: "The coastal health programme delivered 12,400 vaccine doses in May across 18 clinics. Heavy rain delayed transport to 4 clinics for two days, but all planned deliveries were completed by 31 May. A cold-storage unit failed at one site on 14 May; staff moved stock within 40 minutes and no doses were lost. The June plan adds 3 mobile teams to reach remote communities."
process: The system reads the full paragraph and separates the facts into units.
It identifies likely key points: doses delivered, delays, no losses, and the June expansion.
It drops lower-priority detail such as the exact date of the storage failure and the 40-minute transfer time.
It outputs a shorter version in one or two sentences.
workedExample.result: Summary: "In May, the programme delivered 12,400 vaccine doses to 18 clinics. Rain caused short transport delays, but all deliveries were completed, no doses were lost, and June will add 3 mobile teams to reach remote communities."

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A policy officer searches past General Assembly resolutions and requests short summaries of earlier language on a recurring issue before drafting a briefing note.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: This helps staff scan a large set of documents quickly, compare themes across years, and decide which original texts need close review.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Use only approved tools and approved document collections. Do not paste confidential negotiations, unpublished drafts, personal data or other sensitive material into an unapproved public AI service, and always verify quoted language against the source resolution.

whyItMatters: Summarisation matters because most people face more text than they can read in full. A good summary can help you triage documents, prepare for meetings, scan evidence, and find what deserves deeper review. For policy, communications and management work, that can save time and improve consistency. But the value depends on knowing its limits: a short version may omit conditions, caveats or minority views. If you understand the term, you are better able to ask when a summary is suitable, when the original must be checked, and what quality controls are needed.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A summary is just the first few sentences shortened.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Useful summarisation usually tries to identify the most important information across the whole source. In many documents, the key point appears later, is repeated in several places, or depends on context, so simply trimming the start often fails.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If the summary reads well, it must be accurate.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Fluent wording is not proof of faithfulness to the source. A system can produce a clear, polished summary that leaves out a condition, changes emphasis, or adds a detail not supported by the original text.
Some systems extract existing sentences directly from the source, while others generate new wording. Both are called summarisation, but they have different strengths and risks.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: It gives you the shorter version of a long text, keeping the main points and leaving out detail.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Summarisation is a task in natural language processing that maps one or more source documents to a shorter text intended to preserve salient content. Two broad approaches are extractive summarisation, which selects and orders spans such as sentences from the source, and abstractive summarisation, which generates new wording conditioned on the source. Systems may use sentence scoring, attention mechanisms, encoder-decoder architectures, or large language models. Quality is often judged by faithfulness to the source, coverage of key information, coherence, and brevity, though automatic scores do not fully capture factual accuracy or usefulness.

keyTakeaway: Summarisation can save time, but it is a compressed view of the source, not a guarantee of completeness or accuracy.

quickCheck.question: Which option best describes summarisation?
options: Changing a document from one language to another
Producing a shorter version of source content that keeps the main points
Grouping many documents into topics without writing a readable short version
Creating any new text, even without source material
quickCheck.explanation: Summarisation starts from source material and aims to preserve its main information in less space. Translation changes language. Topic modelling finds themes rather than writing a concise account. General text generation may have no source document at all.
